To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the viral oncogene is a regulatory gene, that it is a component of a regulatory gene system which includes the cellular oncogene, the viral regulatory gene, and the cellular regulatory gene, that these regulatory genes play important roles in cellular differentiation and oncogenicity, and that the cellular and the viral regulatory gene systems are interdependent.

the viral regulatory genes and their cellular counterparts are involved in a dynamic equilibrium of host-virus relationship, and that the viral regulatory gene products may play important roles in viral oncogenesis.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the viral genes, as well as the cellular genes, are not only the products of evolution but are also the driving forces in the evolutionary process.
these genes play an important role in the evolutionary processes, which in turn, determine the outcome of host-virus relationship.
these viral genes, as well as the cellular genes they regulate, are the products of the evolution of host-parasites relationship.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolution of viruses has been a continuous and dynamic process, and the evolution of viral genes and viral genomes is an integral part of the evolutionary process of host-virus interactions.
the host-parasite interaction is a dynamic process which has been governed by the evolutionary forces, and that the host-viral regulatory genes play a critical role in the process.

, the evolutionary view of viral quasispices and variants, viral regulatory genes, and cellular genes, has provided us with the most rational and scientific explanation for the origin and pathogenesis of human cancers, and for the etiologies of many infectious diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the viral regulatory genes are not merely "passenger" genes in a parasitic virus, but rather, are essential for the survival of the host-virus relationship, and for the maintenance of the host's normal physiology.
the host-virus interaction is not only a dynamic equilibrium but is also a process of continuous change.
these viral regulatory genes are of paramount importance in the evolutionary processes.
